Carpus
KAR-pus
proper noun (figure)
Greek Karpos ("fruit"). A believer at Troas with whom Paul left his cloak and books (2 Tim 4:13).

📖 Biblical Definition

Carpus was a believer at Troas in whose house the Apostle Paul had left his cloak, his books, and especially the parchments — a detail preserved in one of the most poignant verses of Paul's final letter: "The cloke that I left at Troas with Carpus, when thou comest, bring with thee, and the books, but especially the parchments" (2 Tim 4:13). Of Carpus we know only his name, his city, and that Paul trusted him to keep his belongings. Yet the verse in which he appears is precious for what it reveals of the aged apostle near the end of his life. Writing from a Roman prison, awaiting execution, Paul asks Timothy to bring three things: his cloak (the heavy traveling cloak he would need against the cold of the Roman winter in his dungeon), his books, and especially the parchments (likely portions of the Scriptures or his own writings). The request is intensely human and deeply instructive: the apostle who had written half the New Testament, facing death, still wanted his cloak for warmth and his books and Scriptures for study and comfort. He did not consider that, having attained such heights of revelation and being so near glory, he was beyond the need of the Word; to the end he wanted the parchments — "especially the parchments." Carpus had faithfully kept these things, and Paul trusted him to have done so. The detail testifies both to the reality of the apostle's human need and to the value he placed on the Scriptures to his dying day, and it preserves forever the name of an obscure believer at Troas who had simply, faithfully, kept the things entrusted to him. Carpus stands for the humble faithfulness of keeping what is entrusted — a small service, perhaps, but one the Spirit of God saw fit to record.

A believer at Troas with whom Paul left his cloak, books, and especially the parchments (2 Tim 4:13); the verse reveals the aged apostle near death still wanting warmth and the Scriptures; Carpus models the humble faithfulness of keeping what is entrusted.

CARPUS, proper noun. Greek Karpos ("fruit"); a believer at Troas.

Named once: 2 Tim 4:13, as the one with whom Paul left his cloak, books, and parchments.

Paul, in a Roman prison awaiting death, asks Timothy to bring the cloak (against the winter cold) and especially the parchments (the Scriptures).

The verse reveals the apostle's human need and his lifelong love of the Word, even near the end.

Carpus faithfully kept the things entrusted; the model of humble faithfulness in keeping a trust.

📖 Key Scripture

2 Timothy 4:13 — "The cloke that I left at Troas with Carpus, when thou comest, bring with thee, and the books, but especially the parchments."

2 Timothy 4:6-7 — "For I am now ready to be offered, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith."

Psalm 119:97 — "O how love I thy law! it is my meditation all the day."

Luke 16:10 — "He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Carpus is corrupted only when the precious human detail of 2 Timothy 4:13 is overlooked, when the apostle's dying love of the Scriptures is missed, or when the humble service of keeping a trust is despised as too small to matter.

expand to see more

Precious-detail overlooked. The mention of Carpus and the cloak is easily skimmed as an incidental closing request. It is one of the most human and instructive verses in Paul's writings. The apostle, in a cold Roman dungeon, near execution, asks for his cloak against the winter, and for his books and "especially the parchments" — the Scriptures. Here is a man who had been caught up to the third heaven (2 Cor 12), who had written letters that are themselves Scripture, who was about to depart and be with Christ — and still he wanted the parchments to the end. The verse rebukes any notion that one can outgrow the need of the Word. Paul loved the Scriptures to his dying day; so should we.

Carpus has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal point worth recovering is twofold: the apostle's lifelong, dying love of the Scriptures ("especially the parchments"), and the humble faithfulness of Carpus in keeping what was entrusted to him. He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much (Luke 16:10). Carpus kept a cloak and some books; the Spirit recorded his name. The smallest faithful service, the keeping of a small trust, is not beneath the notice of God.
